## Lab 13 — TPM/OEE, Root Cause and a New Dataset {#sec-lab-tpm-rca}

::: {.lab-overview}
You bring the whole term together on one problem: a Précitech CNC turning cell
that is not making its numbers. You compute **OEE** from a shift log and split the
losses into the **Six Big Losses**; you Pareto the failure modes; you run a
**5-Why and Ishikawa** root-cause analysis; and then you **direct an LLM** to
build a failure classifier on a *new* dataset — the **AI4I 2020 Predictive
Maintenance Dataset** from the UCI repository (CC BY 4.0, 10 000 rows, 5 labelled
failure modes). This is *classification* on a differently-shaped dataset, so the
C-MAPSS recipe from the capstone does not carry over — the point is to show you
can transfer the skill, not copy the code. Tools: **Google Sheets**,
**draw.io**, **Google Colab**.

**AI use:** required for the classifier task; permitted with disclosure
elsewhere. As in the ML module, you must be able to explain every line.
:::

### Learning outcomes

::: {.lab-outcomes}
After this lab you should be able to:

- Compute OEE (availability × performance × quality) from a shift log and
  attribute the losses to the Six Big Losses.
- Build a Pareto chart of failure modes and identify the vital few.
- Run a 5-Why and an Ishikawa (fishbone) analysis using measured process data as
  evidence.
- Direct an LLM to build and evaluate a classifier on an unfamiliar,
  class-imbalanced dataset, and choose metrics that survive the imbalance.
- Write the D4 (root cause) and D5 (corrective action) sections of an 8D report,
  tying model evidence back to the fishbone.
:::

### Prep work

::: {.lab-prep}
- Read Chapter 12 (TPM, OEE, the Six Big Losses) and Chapter 15 (troubleshooting,
  5-Why, Ishikawa, the 8D report).
- Skim your capstone notebook from Labs 9–12 — you reuse the *workflow* (load,
  explore, split, train, evaluate) but not the code.
- Open the [AI4I 2020 dataset page](https://archive.ics.uci.edu/dataset/601/ai4i+2020+predictive+maintenance+dataset)
  and confirm you can download the CSV in the browser. Columns: air temperature,
  process temperature, rotational speed, torque, tool wear, a machine-failure
  flag, and five failure-mode flags — **TWF** (tool wear), **HDF** (heat
  dissipation), **PWF** (power), **OSF** (overstrain), **RNF** (random).
- Download `precitech_shift_log.csv` from FOL (one week of shift records for the
  CNC cell: planned time, downtime events, ideal cycle time, count, scrap).
- Form teams of 2–3.
:::

### Materials & equipment

::: {.lab-materials}
- Computer with internet access
- [**Google Sheets**](https://sheets.google.com/) — OEE calculation and the Pareto chart
- [**draw.io**](https://app.diagrams.net/) — the Ishikawa diagram
- [**Google Colab**](https://colab.research.google.com) — the classifier
- `precitech_shift_log.csv` from FOL
- **AI4I 2020** CSV, downloaded in-browser from UCI
- Chapter 12 OEE definitions and Chapter 15 8D template
:::

### Procedure

::: {.lab-procedure}
**Task 1 — OEE and the Six Big Losses (25 min). *(2 marks)*** From
`precitech_shift_log.csv`, compute availability (run time ÷ planned production
time), performance (ideal cycle time × total count ÷ run time) and quality (good
count ÷ total count), then OEE = the product. Take each downtime and loss entry
in the log and assign it to one of the Six Big Losses (breakdowns, setup &
adjustment, small stops, reduced speed, startup rejects, production rejects).
State which Big Loss is costing the most OEE points.

**Task 2 — Pareto the failure modes (20 min). *(1 mark)*** In the AI4I data,
count how many rows carry each of TWF, HDF, PWF, OSF and RNF. Build a Pareto
chart in Sheets (bars descending, cumulative line). Identify the vital few
failure modes that account for most of the failures, and note where RNF sits and
why that matters.

**Task 3 — 5-Why and Ishikawa (25 min). *(2 marks)*** Take the top failure mode
from Task 2. Run a 5-Why chain and draw an Ishikawa diagram in draw.io with the
six standard bones (machine, method, material, measurement, man, environment).
Use the **measured feature columns as evidence** on the bones — for example,
compare tool wear, torque, rotational speed and the air-vs-process temperature
gap for the failing rows against the healthy rows, and put the numbers on the
diagram.

**Task 4 — Direct an LLM to build a failure classifier (35 min). *(4 marks)***
In Colab, prompt an LLM to build a classifier that predicts the machine-failure
flag from the five process features. You are transferring the capstone workflow,
not its code — this is tabular classification, not time-series RUL regression.
Report a **confusion matrix** and **precision and recall** for the failure class.
The failure rate in AI4I 2020 is about **3.4 %**, so **accuracy is a useless
metric here** — a model that predicts "no failure" every time scores ~96.6 %
accuracy and catches nothing. State explicitly which class-imbalance trap you
hit and how you detected it. **That is the lesson of this task.**

**Task 5 — 8D D4/D5 (15 min). *(1 mark)*** Write the "D4 — root cause" and
"D5 — permanent corrective action" sections of an 8D report for the top failure
mode. Tie the model's feature importances back to specific bones on your Task 3
fishbone, and propose a corrective action that a TPM programme could actually
carry out (an autonomous-maintenance check, a setup standard, a condition limit).
:::

### Deliverables & submission

::: {.lab-deliverables}
One team report (PDF) with: the OEE calculation and Six-Big-Losses attribution;
the failure-mode Pareto chart; the 5-Why chain and the Ishikawa diagram
(draw.io export) with the feature evidence on it; the Colab notebook link with
the confusion matrix, precision/recall and the class-imbalance write-up; and the
D4/D5 sections. Add an AI-use disclosure line. Submit on FOL by the end of the
lab period.
:::

### Rubric

::: {.lab-rubric}
**10 marks total.**

| Deliverable | Marks |
|---|---|
| OEE computed correctly (availability, performance, quality shown separately); every log entry attributed to a Big Loss; largest loss named | 2 |
| Failure-mode Pareto chart correct (descending bars, cumulative line); vital few identified; RNF discussed | 1 |
| 5-Why chain plus a six-bone Ishikawa diagram with measured feature evidence on the bones | 2 |
| Classifier built via LLM direction; confusion matrix and precision/recall reported; class-imbalance trap identified and explained; accuracy correctly rejected as the metric | 4 |
| D4/D5 sections tie feature importances to the fishbone and propose a TPM-executable corrective action | 1 |
:::

### Instructor notes

::: {.lab-instructor}
- **Prep:** generate `precitech_shift_log.csv` with `Rscript R/make_lab_data.R`
  and stage it on FOL; publish the expected OEE and Pareto order from the answer
  key the script prints. Host a copy of the AI4I 2020 CSV on FOL as a fallback in
  case UCI is unreachable from the lab.
- Confirm `archive.ics.uci.edu`, draw.io and Colab are reachable on the lab
  network the day before (firewall-check list in [Teacher preparation]).
- **Marking:** Task 4 is the point of the lab. A team that reports high accuracy
  and stops has missed it — full marks require them to have *noticed* the
  imbalance and switched to precision/recall (or a resampling / class-weight
  fix). Reused C-MAPSS code that does not fit tabular data is a red flag that the
  transfer did not happen.
- This lab is the destination for the capstone stretch goals — see
  [Lab 12](#sec-lab-ml-capstone) instructor notes.
:::

## Lab 14 — Robotic Work-Cell Design in RoboDK for Web {#sec-lab-robodk}

::: {.lab-overview}
A **take-home** lab: released in week 11, due at the end of week 14, done
individually, with a short screen recording as part of the submission. You design
and program the Précitech kitting cell's pick-and-place robot in **RoboDK for
Web** — a free, no-install, in-browser robot simulator with 600+ real arms. It
bookends Lab 1: toy logic in week 1, a real 6-axis industrial arm in week 14. You
close the loop on the course by checking the robot's cycle time against the
**takt time you computed in Lab 4**.

**AI use:** permitted with disclosure. The station layout, the program and the
cycle times must be your own work.
:::

### Learning outcomes

::: {.lab-outcomes}
After this lab you should be able to:

- Jog a 6-axis robot in joint, linear and tool coordinates and recognise
  singularities and joint-limit stops.
- Lay out a work cell and verify that every pick and place point lies inside the
  robot's reach envelope.
- Program a pick-and-place cycle with targets and gripper I/O and read the
  simulated cycle time.
- Compare a simulated cycle time against a required takt time and optimise the
  program to close the gap.
- Compute a minimum safeguarding distance from robot stopping performance and
  select an appropriate safeguard.
:::

### Prep work

::: {.lab-prep}
- Read Chapter 8 (industrial robotics — coordinate systems, the work envelope,
  singularities) and Chapter 6 (machine guarding — the minimum-distance /
  safeguarding-distance formula and the safeguard hierarchy).
- Have your **Lab 4** takt calculation to hand — you need the takt time for
  250 kits/day.
- Open [RoboDK for Web](https://web.robodk.com/simulation) and confirm it loads
  and runs a sample station in your browser. No account or licence key is
  required.
- Confirm your screen-recording tool works (the same tool the course plan's
  take-home lab uses).
:::

### Materials & equipment

::: {.lab-materials}
- Personal computer with internet access and a browser (this is a take-home lab —
  no lab PC required)
- [RoboDK for Web](https://web.robodk.com/simulation) — no install, no licence
  key
- A screen-recording tool — the built-in recorder is enough (Windows **Xbox Game
  Bar**, <kbd>Win</kbd>+<kbd>G</kbd>; macOS **Screenshot**,
  <kbd>Shift</kbd>+<kbd>Cmd</kbd>+<kbd>5</kbd>) or free [OBS Studio](https://obsproject.com/)
- Your Lab 4 takt time; the [Précitech case study](#sec-precitech-case) (250
  kits/day, one 8-hour shift)
:::

### Procedure

::: {.lab-procedure}
**Task 1 — Jog and observe (20 min). *(1 mark)*** Load a 6-axis arm from the
RoboDK library (any mid-size industrial arm; state which). Jog it in **joint**,
**linear** and **tool** coordinates. Drive it toward a wrist singularity and
toward a joint limit and record what the simulator does in each case. Relate this
back to the robot-programming work in [Lab 1](#sec-lab-logic) and to the Chapter 8
coordinate systems.

**Task 2 — Build the kitting cell (30 min). *(2 marks)*** Assemble the Précitech
kitting cell around the robot: an infeed conveyor delivering shaft blanks, a
bearing-press station, and a tray to be filled. Place a pick point and every
place point. Check that **every pick and place point is inside the reach
envelope**; record the one reach limit that forces you to move a station, and
show the before/after positions.

**Task 3 — Program the pick-and-place (30 min). *(3 marks)*** Create targets and
a program that picks a blank from the conveyor, moves it to the press, then
places the finished part in the tray, with gripper open/close on digital output.
Run it. Record the **simulated cycle time** for one part.

**Task 4 — Cycle time vs takt (25 min). *(3 marks)*** Take the **takt time from
Lab 4** for 250 kits/day. Does one robot at your Task 3 cycle time meet takt?
Then optimise — reorder targets, raise joint speeds within limits, shorten
approach and retract moves — and record the improved cycle time. State by how
much you beat or missed takt, and what a real cell would do if one robot could
not keep up.

**Task 5 — Safeguarding distance (15 min). *(1 mark)*** Using the Chapter 6
minimum-distance formula, compute the minimum guarding distance from an assumed
robot-plus-sensor stopping time (state your assumption). State which Chapter 6
safeguard you would specify for this cell (fixed guard, interlocked gate,
light curtain, area scanner, two-hand control) and why.
:::

### Deliverables & submission

::: {.lab-deliverables}
Submit on FOL by the end of week 14: a report (PDF) covering all five tasks with
the reach-envelope evidence, the cycle-time and takt comparison, and the
safeguarding calculation; **the RoboDK station file**; and a **screen recording
(3–5 min)** showing the program running and you talking through one design
decision. Add an AI-use disclosure line.
:::

### Rubric

::: {.lab-rubric}
**10 marks total.**

| Deliverable | Marks |
|---|---|
| Jogging in joint / linear / tool coordinates demonstrated; singularity and joint-limit behaviour recorded | 1 |
| Kitting cell built; every pick/place point verified inside the reach envelope; the binding reach limit and the layout change recorded | 2 |
| Working pick-and-place program with targets and gripper I/O; runs in the simulator; cycle time reported | 3 |
| Cycle time compared against the Lab 4 takt; one round of optimisation with the improved time and the gap quantified | 3 |
| Minimum safeguarding distance computed from a stated stopping time; a specific Chapter 6 safeguard chosen and justified | 1 |
:::

### Instructor notes

::: {.lab-instructor}
- **Release in week 11** alongside Lab 11, so students have the full three weeks;
  it is due at the end of week 14. This mirrors the course plan's existing
  take-home lab pattern (released three weeks out, video submission).
- **Prep:** the day before release, run through Tasks 1–3 in RoboDK for Web
  yourself on the college network — confirm `web.robodk.com` is reachable, the
  library loads, and a station can be saved and re-loaded. Have a reference
  station file and an expected cycle-time range (from the answer key in
  `R/make_lab_data.R` output) ready for marking.
- No lab room is needed — this is done from home — but reserve 15 minutes in the
  week-11 lab to demo the tool and walk through the brief.
- **Marking:** the takt comparison in Task 4 only works if the student's Lab 4
  takt was correct; if it was not, mark Task 4 on the *method* against a takt you
  supply. Watch for cycle times that are physically implausible (joint speeds
  cranked past limits) — that is where the "your own work" line is tested.
:::

### Appendix: instrumentation-trainer lab stream

An older set of labs for this course code was written for the **B1033** trainer
benches (author "MZhang"). They are **not** part of the current lab set, but the
handouts are in the `LabInstructions/` folder and are summarised here in case the
course runs them:

| Alt lab | Title | Room | Equipment | Software |
|----|----|----|----|----|
| Alt — Pressure/level | Pressure Measurement for Level | B1033 | Trainer: power-supply module, pump/tank unit, RTD temperature transmitter, pressure transmitter, float/reed switch, 2 × DMM, banana leads | — |
| Alt — Motor control | Motor Control & Intro to VFDs | B1033 | 3-phase motor, FVNR (full-voltage non-reversing) starters, control-relay/MCR wiring, E-stop, pilot lights, pushbuttons; VFD | — |
| Alt — PLC | PLC Introduction with Siemens | B1033 | Siemens PLC trainer, field devices (pushbuttons, selector switches, pilot lights, cylinders with proxy sensors), potentiometer 0–10 VDC, DMM | **Siemens TIA Portal**; reference video `YOvQhvjaeqY` |
| Alt — Flow rate | Flow Rate Measurement | B1033 | Trainer: pump/tank unit, paddle-wheel flow transmitter, rotameter (LPM/GPM), RTD temperature transmitter, 2 × DMM, hoses/banana leads | — |

Prep for the alt stream: book **B1033**; confirm every trainer bench has a
working power-supply module, pump/tank unit and the two DMMs; confirm **Siemens
TIA Portal** licences for the PLC lab; print each handout's instructor sign-off
sheet (4 sign-offs per lab).
